question: Slicing an onion releases a gas that stings your eyes. Which chemical element is at the heart of that gas? It's the same one behind the smell of rotten eggs and struck matches.
source_excerpt: a member of a class of organosulfur compounds known as thiocarbonyl S-oxides... is a volatile liquid that acts as a lachrymatory agent

extra.why_interesting: Everyone has cried over onions, but few know what causes it. The clues about rotten eggs and matches give a fair way to reason to the element.
extra.verification_notes: The onion lachrymatory factor, syn-propanethial S-oxide (C3H6OS), is an organosulfur compound, and rotten-egg (H2S) and match (sulfur/SO2) smells also come from sulfur.

explanation: Cutting the onion breaks open its cells, and enzymes convert its sulfur compounds into an irritating gas. Your eyes then flood with tears to wash it away, which is why chilling the onion first helps.

question: At sea level, water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. At roughly what temperature does it boil on the summit of Mount Everest?
source_excerpt: Although water boils at 100°C at sea level, the boiling point on top of Mount Everest is only about 70°C.

extra.why_interesting: People assume water boils at 100 °C everywhere. On Everest it boils about 30 degrees cooler, too cool to cook food properly.
extra.verification_notes: Summit pressure is about a third of sea level, giving a boiling point of roughly 68–71 °C, so 'about 70 °C' is correct (Lumen Learning chemistry text).

explanation: With only about a third of sea-level air pressure pushing down, water boils at around 70 degrees on Everest. That's why climbers' tea is lukewarm and pasta never cooks properly up there.

question: Many household smoke detectors contain a tiny speck of a radioactive element named after a continent. Which element is it?
source_excerpt: it is the one actinide that is found in almost every household: as an isotope that produces ionizing radiation, it is an essential component of smoke detectors.

extra.why_interesting: Few people realise a radioactive element sits on their ceiling. The 'named after a continent' clue narrows the field to a fair guess.
extra.verification_notes: Americium-241 is the standard ionization smoke detector source and the element is named after the Americas; no competing continent-named element is used in smoke detectors, and nothing newer changes this.

explanation: Americium-241 gives off particles that make the air inside the detector conduct a tiny current. Smoke interrupts that current and sets off the alarm, and the amount inside is far too small to harm you.

question: True or false: old cathedral windows are thicker at the bottom because glass is really a very slow-flowing liquid that has sagged over the centuries.
source_excerpt: much too high to observe measurable viscous flow on human time scale

extra.why_interesting: This is a widely repeated 'science fact' that many players will confidently call true. Busting it is the payoff.
extra.verification_notes: Glass viscosity calculations show no observable flow in medieval windows; uneven thickness comes from manufacturing, so 'False' is correct (https://ceramics.org/ceramic-tech-today/glass-viscosity-calculations-definitively-debunk-the-myth-of-observable-flow-in-medieval-windows/).

explanation: False. Medieval panes came out uneven, and glaziers often fitted the heavy edge at the bottom. At room temperature, glass wouldn't visibly sag even over the age of the universe.

question: When yeast feeds on the sugars in bread dough, it gives off a gas that makes the dough rise. Which gas?
source_excerpt: Enzymes in yeast ferment sugar forming carbon dioxide and ethanol. The carbon dioxide makes the bread rise

extra.why_interesting: This is an easy warm-up with a real payoff. The holes in your bread are trapped gas, and the 'alcohol' bakes off in the oven.
extra.verification_notes: Yeast ferments sugars into CO2 and ethanol; the CO2 makes dough rise, per the RSC (https://edu.rsc.org/experiments/yeast-and-the-expansion-of-bread-dough/1748.article).

explanation: The holes in a slice of bread are bubbles of carbon dioxide trapped by stretchy gluten. Yeast also makes a little alcohol, which mostly evaporates in the oven.

question: In 1945, an American engineer noticed a chocolate bar melting in his pocket while he stood beside equipment for which military technology, a discovery that led to the microwave oven?
source_excerpt: In 1945, Spencer noticed that a candy bar in his pocket had mysteriously melted while testing an active magnetron.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the microwave oven as a deliberate kitchen invention. In fact it came from wartime military hardware and a ruined snack. The chocolate detail and the 1945 date give enough footholds to reason toward wartime radar.
extra.verification_notes: Percy Spencer (Raytheon) noticed a candy bar melting in 1945 near a radar magnetron, which led to the microwave oven; radar is correct (https://www.history.com/articles/microwave-oven-invention).

explanation: Percy Spencer of Raytheon was working near a magnetron, the tube that produced microwaves for radar sets. Raytheon's first microwave oven, the 'Radarange', stood almost 1.8 metres tall and weighed around 340 kilograms.
